newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: RUGBY UNION-ASHTON ASSUMES ROLE AS IRELAND SAVIOUR.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-ASHTON ASSUMES ROLE AS IRELAND SAVIOUR.

text.p: Brian Ashton's role as the possible saviour of Irish rugby union began in earnest on Thursday the Irish Development squad took off on a seven match tour of New Zealand and Western Samoa.
"Up to now, I feel as if I have been holding someone else's baby," Ashton said.
Ashton, 50, was appointed coaching advisor to the Ireland team within four days of quitting as coach of English club champions Bath in January.
The Ireland squad he inherited was in need of fresh impetus and inspiration having lost six of their previous seven internationals, including humiliating home defeats by Western Samoa and Italy.
But Ashton barely had time to get to know some of his players' names before the Five Nations' championship was underway.
Four games later and the Irish had picked up the wooden spoon having won only one of their championship outings, that against Wales in Cardiff.
In the seven Test matches Ireland played this season they scored 102 points while conceding 240, scoring just six tries and conceding 28.
Ireland used 34 players in those seven matches.
Ashton did not try to disguise his displeasure with the Irish players after they were trashed 38-10 in their final championship game by Scotland in Murrayfield.
"There was no excuse for today's performance. In the second half I was bitterly disappointed - almost to the point of embarrassment," he said.

Ashton, who was officially appointed as full-time Irish coach until the end of the 2003 World Cup last month, will use the Development Tour to work with his players and teach them the realities of rugby life in the professional age.
"It means working nine-to-five, going out to play on Saturday and if you're lucky, getting Sunday off," Ashton said.

"I suspect a lot of them (Irish players) train two or three times a week, play a few video games, watch a bit of television and go down to the pub. This is miles away from what we're looking for," he added.
Ashton is likely to learn a great deal about the potential and attitude, both on and off the field, of his players on this tour.
What he wants is to see Ireland play a brand of 15-man rugby, with a topping of Irish passion.

With four of Ireland's top players, Keith Wood, Paul Wallace, Jeremy Davidson and Eric Miller in the British Lions squad who depart for South Africa this weekend, those players on the peripherary of the team will have a chance to impress.

Although Ireland will play only one Test match, when they will re-new rivalry with Western Samoa in their final game of the tour in Apia on June 14 and do not play any of the major provincial sides in New Zealand, Ireland face some stiff challenges ahead.
"No matter what we call it, 'A' Tour, 'Development' Tour, the New Zealanders will bill it as Ireland versus whoever," Ashton said.
"We have got to get on with the show, deal with the players at our disposal and play the game," he added.
